claim: Genetic disruption of the Vacuolar H+ ATPase (V-ATPase) stabilizes HIF1α in aerobic conditions.
source: Here, we use an unbiased genome-wide genetic screen in near-haploid human cells to uncover cellular processes that regulate HIF1α. We identify that genetic disruption of the Vacuolar H+ ATPase (V-ATPase), the key proton pump for endo-lysosomal acidification, and two previously uncharacterised V-ATPase assembly factors, TMEM199 and CCDC115, stabilise HIF1α in aerobic conditions.
evidence: Supported by the forward genetic screen results showing enrichment of V-ATPase subunit mutations in cells with elevated HIF1α levels, and validated by CRISPR-Cas9 experiments.

claim: TMEM199 and CCDC115 are previously uncharacterized V-ATPase assembly factors that stabilize HIF1α in aerobic conditions when disrupted.
source: Here, we use an unbiased genome-wide genetic screen in near-haploid human cells to uncover cellular processes that regulate HIF1α. We identify that genetic disruption of the Vacuolar H+ ATPase (V-ATPase), the key proton pump for endo-lysosomal acidification, and two previously uncharacterised V-ATPase assembly factors, TMEM199 and CCDC115, stabilise HIF1α in aerobic conditions.
evidence: Supported by genetic screen data, CRISPR validation experiments, and co-immunoprecipitation showing association with V-ATPase subunits.

claim: Disrupting the V-ATPase results in intracellular iron depletion rather than preventing lysosomal degradation of HIF1α.
source: Rather than preventing the lysosomal degradation of HIF1α, disrupting the V-ATPase results in intracellular iron depletion, thereby impairing PHD activity and leading to HIF activation.
evidence: Supported by IRP2 accumulation data, in vitro hydroxylation assays, and iron supplementation rescue experiments.

claim: V-ATPase disruption impairs PHD activity by depleting intracellular iron.
source: Rather than preventing the lysosomal degradation of HIF1α, disrupting the V-ATPase results in intracellular iron depletion, thereby impairing PHD activity and leading to HIF activation.
evidence: Supported by in vitro hydroxylation assays showing reduced PHD activity in BafA-treated lysates and restoration with iron supplementation.

claim: Iron supplementation directly restores PHD catalytic activity following V-ATPase inhibition.
source: Iron supplementation directly restores PHD catalytic activity following V-ATPase inhibition, revealing important links between the V-ATPase, iron metabolism and HIFs.
evidence: Supported by in vitro hydroxylation assays and cellular experiments showing HIF1α degradation is restored with iron citrate treatment.

claim: HIFα is constitutively expressed but rapidly degraded by the proteasome in aerobic conditions.
source: In aerobic conditions, the HIFα subunit is constitutively expressed but rapidly degraded by the proteasome, in a process requiring two post-translational modifications: (i) prolyl hydroxylation of the HIFα oxygen dependent degradation (ODD) domain by prolyl hydroxylases (PHDs) (Bruick and McKnight, 2001; Epstein et al., 2001), and (ii) subsequent ubiquitination by the von-hippel lindau (VHL) E3 ligase (Maxwell et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on HIF regulation.

claim: Prolyl hydroxylation of HIFα by PHDs is required for proteasomal degradation in aerobic conditions.
source: In aerobic conditions, the HIFα subunit is constitutively expressed but rapidly degraded by the proteasome, in a process requiring two post-translational modifications: (i) prolyl hydroxylation of the HIFα oxygen dependent degradation (ODD) domain by prolyl hydroxylases (PHDs) (Bruick and McKnight, 2001; Epstein et al., 2001), and (ii) subsequent ubiquitination by the von-hippel lindau (VHL) E3 ligase (Maxwell et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational studies on PHD-mediated HIF regulation.

claim: VHL E3 ligase ubiquitinates HIFα following prolyl hydroxylation.
source: In aerobic conditions, the HIFα subunit is constitutively expressed but rapidly degraded by the proteasome, in a process requiring two post-translational modifications: (i) prolyl hydroxylation of the HIFα oxygen dependent degradation (ODD) domain by prolyl hydroxylases (PHDs) (Bruick and McKnight, 2001; Epstein et al., 2001), and (ii) subsequent ubiquitination by the von-hippel lindau (VHL) E3 ligase (Maxwell et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maxwell et al., 1999 establishing VHL's role in HIF ubiquitination.

claim: Prolyl hydroxylation of HIFα acts as the recruitment signal for VHL.
source: Prolyl hydroxylation of HIFα acts as the recruitment signal for VHL, which rapidly ubiquitinates the ODD domain facilitating proteasomal degradation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the HIF-VHL pathway.

claim: HIF1α is a very short-lived protein.
source: Indeed, HIF1α (the ubiquitously expressed HIFα isoform) is a very short-lived protein (Berra et al., 2001), and the efficiency of VHL in promoting proteasomal degradation has led to the recent development of small molecules that hijack the VHL complex to selectively destroy target proteins as a potential therapeutic tool (Bondeson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berra et al., 2001.

claim: The efficiency of VHL in promoting proteasomal degradation has led to the development of small molecules that hijack the VHL complex to selectively destroy target proteins.
source: Indeed, HIF1α (the ubiquitously expressed HIFα isoform) is a very short-lived protein (Berra et al., 2001), and the efficiency of VHL in promoting proteasomal degradation has led to the recent development of small molecules that hijack the VHL complex to selectively destroy target proteins as a potential therapeutic tool (Bondeson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bondeson et al., 2015.

claim: Lysosomal inhibitors can lead to stabilization of HIFα in both normal oxygen levels and in hypoxia.
source: Despite this clear role for proteasomal degradation of HIF, it has been reported that lysosomal inhibitors can lead to stabilisation of the HIFα subunit in both normal oxygen levels and in hypoxia.
evidence: Based on prior literature reports.

claim: Lysosomal inhibitor-mediated stabilization of HIFα can lead to a functional HIF response.
source: Moreover, this stabilisation can lead to a functional HIF response (Lim et al., 2006), and upregulation of target genes to promote glucose metabolism and angiogenesis (Hubbi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lim et al., 2006 and Hubbi et al., 2013.

claim: Bafilomycin A treatment stabilizes HIF1α and prevents its degradation.
source: BafA treatment stabilised HIF1α and prevented its degradation (Lim et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lim et al., 2006 and confirmed by experimental data in this study.

claim: Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain HIF1 stabilization upon BafA treatment, including chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA).
source: Others report similar findings, with several proposed mechanisms to explain the stabilisation of HIF1 upon BafA treatment, including chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) (Bremm et al., 2014; Ferreira et al., 2015; Hubbi et al., 2014, 2013; Selfridge et al., 2016), mitochondrial uncoupling (Zhdanov et al., 2012) and binding of the V-ATPase to VHL (Lim et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mitochondrial uncoupling has been proposed as a mechanism for HIF1 stabilization upon BafA treatment.
source: Others report similar findings, with several proposed mechanisms to explain the stabilisation of HIF1 upon BafA treatment, including chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) (Bremm et al., 2014; Ferreira et al., 2015; Hubbi et al., 2014, 2013; Selfridge et al., 2016), mitochondrial uncoupling (Zhdanov et al., 2012) and binding of the V-ATPase to VHL (Lim et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhdanov et al., 2012.

claim: Binding of the V-ATPase to VHL has been proposed as a mechanism for HIF1 stabilization upon BafA treatment.
source: Others report similar findings, with several proposed mechanisms to explain the stabilisation of HIF1 upon BafA treatment, including chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) (Bremm et al., 2014; Ferreira et al., 2015; Hubbi et al., 2014, 2013; Selfridge et al., 2016), mitochondrial uncoupling (Zhdanov et al., 2012) and binding of the V-ATPase to VHL (Lim et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lim et al., 2007.

claim: Mutations in several V-ATPase subunits result in increased HIF1α levels.
source: Here, we used this screen to focus on cellular pathways enriched for gene-trapping insertions, and find that mutations in several V-ATPase subunits result in increased HIF1α levels.
evidence: Supported by forward genetic screen data showing enrichment of V-ATPase subunit mutations.

claim: TMEM199 and CCDC115 form the mammalian orthologue of the yeast Vma12p-Vma22p V-ATPase assembly complex.
source: In addition, we identify two uncharacterised V-ATPase accessory proteins, TMEM199 and CCDC115, which we show are required for V-ATPase function and form the mammalian orthologue of the yeast Vma12p-Vma22p V-ATPase assembly complex.
evidence: Supported by sequence homology, co-immunoprecipitation data, and functional assays showing their requirement for V-ATPase function.

claim: TMEM199 and CCDC115 are required for V-ATPase function.
source: In addition, we identify two uncharacterised V-ATPase accessory proteins, TMEM199 and CCDC115, which we show are required for V-ATPase function and form the mammalian orthologue of the yeast Vma12p-Vma22p V-ATPase assembly complex.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing impaired endosomal acidification and lysosomal degradation when these proteins are depleted.

claim: The V-ATPase is required for lysosomal degradation.
source: Although the V-ATPase is required for lysosomal degradation (Maxson and Grinstein, 2014), we find that the mechanism for HIF1α stabilisation following V-ATPase inhibition is through intracellular iron depletion, leading to decreased PHD activity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Maxson and Grinstein, 2014 and established knowledge.

claim: Five V-ATPase subunits were enriched for gene-trapping insertions in the forward genetic screen: ATP6AP1, ATP6V1A, ATP6V1G1, ATP6V0A2 and ATP6V0D1.
source: However, the top ranked biological process was transferrin transport and V-ATPase function (Figure 1B), principally relating to mutagenesis of genes encoding five V-ATPase subunits: ATP6AP1, ATP6V1A, ATP6V1G1, ATP6V0A2 and ATP6V0D1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by the forward genetic screen data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: V-ATPase gene-trap inserts were enriched for mutations in a trapping orientation, consistent with deletion phenotypes.
source: Subsequent analysis of the location of V-ATPase gene-trap inserts confirmed that these genes were enriched for mutations in a trapping orientation (Figure 1C), consistent with mutations resulting in deletion phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by analysis of gene-trap insertion sites shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Depletion of V-ATPase subunits by CRISPR-Cas9 increases GFP levels in HIF1α-GFPODD reporter cells.
source: Depletion of all of the V-ATPase subunits identified in the screen increased GFP levels in the sgRNA-targeted cells compared with the wildtype cells and control sgRNA to MHC Class I (β2 microglobulin, β2m) (Figure 1D), but to a lesser extent than depletion of the main PHD enzyme for HIF1α, PHD2 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Depletion of V-ATPase subunits increases endogenous HIF1α levels.
source: Depletion of the V-ATPase subunits also increased endogenous HIF1α, depending on the efficiency of the sgRNA (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Chemical inhibition of V-ATPase activity with Bafilomycin A activates the HIF1α-GFPODD reporter and increases HIF1α levels in aerobic conditions.
source: Furthermore, chemical inhibition of V-ATPase activity with the inhibitor Bafilomycin A (BafA) activated the GFP reporter, increasing HIF1α levels in aerobic conditions (Figure 1F,G) without affecting HIF1α mRNA expression (see Figure 9J).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 1F, 1G, and 9J.

claim: Bafilomycin A treatment does not affect HIF1α mRNA expression.
source: Furthermore, chemical inhibition of V-ATPase activity with the inhibitor Bafilomycin A (BafA) activated the GFP reporter, increasing HIF1α levels in aerobic conditions (Figure 1F,G) without affecting HIF1α mRNA expression (see Figure 9J).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 9J.

claim: TMEM199 was significantly enriched for gene-trapping insertions in the forward genetic screen.
source: In addition to the V-ATPase subunits detected in the screen, we identified that TMEM199 was significantly enriched for gene-trapping insertions (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by genetic screen data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TMEM199 is a putative transmembrane protein with 24% sequence identity to the yeast V-ATPase assembly protein Vma12p.
source: TMEM199 is a putative transmembrane protein with homology (24% sequence identity) to the yeast V-ATPase assembly protein Vma12p (also known as Vph2p) (Hirata et al., 1993) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis and citation to Hirata et al., 1993.

claim: Depletion of TMEM199 results in accumulation of the HIF1α reporter.
source: Depletion of TMEM199 resulted in accumulation of the HIF1α reporter (Figure 2C), similarly to levels observed for depletion of the V-ATPase subunits (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Endogenous HIF1α only accumulates in the GFPHIGH population of TMEM199 sgRNA-targeted cells.
source: FACS of the GFPLOW and GFPHIGH TMEM199 sgRNA-targeted cells followed by immunoblot showed that endogenous HIF1α only accumulated in the GFPHIGH population (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by FACS and immunoblot data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Overexpression of CRISPR-resistant TMEM199 reverses HIF1α accumulation in TMEM199 sgRNA-targeted cells.
source: Moreover, when we overexpressed a CRISPR resistant TMEM199 in these TMEM199 sgRNA-targeted cells, the accumulation of HIF1α was reversed (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E demonstrating rescue of the phenotype.

claim: Most TMEM199 knockout clones are lethal after three weeks.
source: We also isolated TMEM199 knockout (KO) clones, and while most TMEM199 knockouts were lethal after three weeks, a small number of clones that showed undetectable levels of endogenous TMEM199 by immunoblot had elevated HIF1α levels despite several passages (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations during clonal isolation.

claim: TMEM199 knockout clones with undetectable TMEM199 levels have elevated HIF1α levels.
source: We also isolated TMEM199 knockout (KO) clones, and while most TMEM199 knockouts were lethal after three weeks, a small number of clones that showed undetectable levels of endogenous TMEM199 by immunoblot had elevated HIF1α levels despite several passages (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Reconstituting TMEM199 knockout clones with overexpressed TMEM199 decreases HIF1α levels.
source: Reconstituting these clonal cells with overexpressed TMEM199 decreased HIF1α levels (Figure 2F), further confirming the effect of TMEM199 depletion on HIF1α accumulation.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2F demonstrating rescue.

claim: Human TMEM199 mutations have been associated with glycosylation defects.
source: Human TMEM199 mutations have been recently associated with glycosylation defects (Jansen et al., 2016c), but the role of TMEM199 in V-ATPase function was not known.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jansen et al., 2016c.

claim: TMEM199 associates with V-ATPase subunits ATP6V0D1 and ATP6V0A2.
source: Six proteins were identified as associating with TMEM199 with high confidence compared to the TMEM199 KO cells (Figure 2G). Of these, two were V-ATPase subunits, ATP6V0D1 and ATP6V0A2, which were also identified in the genetic screen (Figure 1A,C), and have been shown to associate with Vma12p in yeast (Graham et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2G and citation to Graham et al., 1998.

claim: CCDC115 shows high structural homology to the yeast V-ATPase assembly factor Vma22p.
source: A further protein, CCDC115 (coiled-coil domain-containing protein 115), was of particular interest as a 3-dimensional structural prediction analysis (Kelley et al., 2015) showed high structural homology to the yeast V-ATPase assembly factor Vma22p (Figure 2H) known to bind Vma12p (Graham et al., 1998), and human mutations in CCDC115 have been recently reported to show glycosylation defects (Jansen et al., 2016b) similarly to the TMEM199 mutations.
evidence: Supported by structural prediction analysis shown in Figure 2H and citations.

claim: Human mutations in CCDC115 show glycosylation defects.
source: A further protein, CCDC115 (coiled-coil domain-containing protein 115), was of particular interest as a 3-dimensional structural prediction analysis (Kelley et al., 2015) showed high structural homology to the yeast V-ATPase assembly factor Vma22p (Figure 2H) known to bind Vma12p (Graham et al., 1998), and human mutations in CCDC115 have been recently reported to show glycosylation defects (Jansen et al., 2016b) similarly to the TMEM199 mutations.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jansen et al., 2016b.

claim: TMEM199 and FLAG-tagged CCDC115 interact as shown by immunoprecipitation.
source: Immunoprecipitation of endogenous TMEM199 with FLAG-tagged CCDC115 confirmed the interaction identified by mass spectrometry (Figure 2I), and depleting CCDC115 from HeLa HIF1α-GFPODD cells stabilised the fluorescent reporter and endogenous HIF1α similarly to TMEM199 deletion (Figure 2J,K).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Depleting CCDC115 stabilizes the HIF1α-GFPODD reporter and endogenous HIF1α similarly to TMEM199 deletion.
source: Immunoprecipitation of endogenous TMEM199 with FLAG-tagged CCDC115 confirmed the interaction identified by mass spectrometry (Figure 2I), and depleting CCDC115 from HeLa HIF1α-GFPODD cells stabilised the fluorescent reporter and endogenous HIF1α similarly to TMEM199 deletion (Figure 2J,K).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 2J and 2K.

claim: Yeast Vma12p-Vma22p localize to the endoplasmic reticulum where they are involved in V-ATPase assembly.
source: Yeast Vma12p-Vma22p localise to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where they are thought to be involved in V-ATPase assembly (Graham et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graham et al., 1998.

claim: TMEM199 is only present in the total membrane pool and not in the soluble fraction.
source: Using cell fractionation experiments we observed that TMEM199 was only present in the total membrane pool and not in the soluble fraction (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by cell fractionation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TMEM199 localizes predominantly to the ER rather than endosomal or lysosomal compartments.
source: Furthermore, immunofluorescence microscopy showed endogenous TMEM199 localised predominantly to the ER, rather than endosomal or lysosomal compartments (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Endogenous TMEM199 co-localizes with HA-CCDC115 at the ER, although CCDC115 is mostly cytosolic.
source: While it was not possible to visualise endogenous CCDC115 by immunoblot or fluorescence microscopy, we observed co-localisation of endogenous TMEM199 with HA-CCDC115 at the ER, although CCDC115 is mostly cytosolic (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: TMEM199 and CCDC115 form a complex at the ER, analogous to the yeast Vma12p-Vma22p V-ATPase assembly proteins.
source: These results suggest that TMEM199 and CCDC115 form a complex at the ER, analogous to the yeast Vma12p-Vma22p V-ATPase assembly proteins (Graham et al., 1998).
evidence: Inferred from localization data, co-immunoprecipitation, and homology to yeast proteins.

claim: TMEM199 and CCDC115 deficient cells prevent EGFR degradation following EGF stimulation.
source: EGF treatment stimulated the degradation of EGFR at 45 min in the control cells, with near complete loss of the receptor by 3 hr, consistent with prior reports (Mizuno et al., 2005) (Figure 4A–C). This degradation was prevented with BafA treatment (Figure 4A), confirming the role of the V-ATPase in the degradation of EGFR. However, EGF had no effect on the levels of EGFR in the TMEM199 or CCDC15 null cells, and no degradation was detected over 3 hr (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Supported by EGFR degradation assay data shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: TMEM199 and CCDC115 deficient cells prevent EGFR degradation similarly to BafA treatment.
source: Indeed, TMEM199 and CCDC115 deficient cells prevented EGFR degradation similarly to BafA treatment (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by comparison of EGFR degradation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Depletion of TMEM199, CCDC115, or core V-ATPase subunits partially rescues MHC Class I at the cell surface in K3-expressing cells.
source: Therefore, we used HeLa cells expressing K3, which have low resting levels of cell surface MHC Class I (Figure 4D), and transduced these cells with sgRNA targeting TMEM199, CCDC115 or core V-ATPase subunits (ATP6V1A1, ATP6V0D1). Mixed populations of TMEM199 or CCDC115 deficient cells partially rescued MHC Class I at the cell surface (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: V-ATPase inhibition with BafA prevents acidification of endosomal compartments.
source: However, live cell microscopy of HIF1α-mCherryODD reporter cells treated with BafA revealed Tfnr-phl within intracellular vesicles, confirming that V-ATPase inhibition prevented acidification of endosomal compartments (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by live cell microscopy data using pH-sensitive Tfnr-phl shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: TMEM199 or CCDC115 depletion prevents acidification of endosomes.
source: Thus, TMEM199 and CCDC115 depletion prevents acidification of endosomes, similarly to BafA treatment or depletion of core V-ATPase subunits.
evidence: Supported by Tfnr-phl fluorescence data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: V-ATPase inhibitors and the proteasome inhibitor MG132 result in similar levels of HIF1α accumulation.
source: We therefore measured the levels of HIF1α in HeLa cells treated with different V-ATPase inhibitors in comparison to the proteasome inhibitor, MG132 (Figure 6A). Surprisingly, we observed similar levels of HIF1α accumulation following treatment with either V-ATPase inhibitors or MG132.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: BafA treatment increases HIF1α levels after just 4 hours.
source: Furthermore, BafA treatment increased HIF1α levels after just 4 hr (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by time-course immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HIF1α is only observed in the nuclei of cells treated with BafA or depleted of TMEM199.
source: Rather than observing HIF1α accumulation within endosomal-lysosomal compartments, as would be expected following disruption of the V-ATPase, HIF1α was only observed in the nuclei of cells treated with BafA (Figure 6C) or depleted of TMEM199 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: Nuclear increase in HIF1α following V-ATPase disruption is sufficient to activate HIF responsive genes.
source: This nuclear increase in HIF1α was sufficient to activate HIF responsive genes, demonstrated by an increase in cell surface and total Carbonic Anhydrase 9 (CA9) when cells were depleted of TMEM199, CCDC115 or core V-ATPase subunits (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: V-ATPase inhibition or depletion stabilizes HIF2α and the HIF target gene Heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1).
source: V-ATPase inhibition or depletion also stabilised HIF2α in HeLa cells and the HIF target gene Heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1) (Bertout et al., 2009) (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6G and citation to Bertout et al., 2009.

claim: Depletion of HSC70, LAMP2A, or ATG16 has no effect on HIF1α stabilization in aerobic conditions.
source: To determine if CMA or macroautophagy played a significant role in the regulation of HIF1α in aerobic conditions, we examined the effect of depletion of HSC70, LAMP2A and ATG16 on HIF1α levels. Depletion of the CMA mediators, HSC70 and LAMP2A, or loss of the macroautophagy protein, ATG16, had no effect on HIF1α stabilisation in aerobic conditions (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 7A-C.

claim: BafA treatment still stabilizes HIF1α even when LAMP2A, HSC70, or ATG16 are depleted.
source: Moreover, BafA treatment still stabilised HIF1α even when LAMP2A, HSC70 or ATG16 were depleted (Figure 7A,C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 7A, 7C, and 7D.

claim: Only MG132 results in the accumulation of prolyl-hydroxylated HIF1α, while BafA and chloroquine stabilize HIF1α in a non-hydroxylated form.
source: We measured the levels of total and prolyl-hydroxylated HIF1α in HeLa cells treated with several V-ATPase inhibitors, the proteasome inhibitor MG132, or the PHD inhibitor DMOG (dimethyloxaloylglycine) using a HIF1α prolyl hydroxyl-specific antibody (Figure 7E,F). While all inhibitors increased total HIF1α levels, only MG132 resulted in the accumulation of prolyl-hydroxylated HIF1α (Figure 7E,F). Conversely, BafA and chloroquine stabilised HIF1α in a non-hydroxylated form, similarly to DMOG treatment (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: BafA treatment markedly reduces PHD-mediated hydroxylation of HIF1αODD in vitro.
source: Lysates from wildtype HeLa cells or cells treated with BafA for 24 hr were incubated with a purified His-tagged HIF1αODD protein for 15 min, and hydroxylation measured using the hydroxyprolyl-specific antibody. While HIF1αODD was rapidly hydroxylated in the wildtype HeLa lysate, BafA treatment markedly reduced hydroxylation (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: Supported by in vitro hydroxylation assay data shown in Figures 7G and 7H.

claim: V-ATPase inhibition stabilizes HIF1α by decreasing PHD enzymatic activity rather than preventing lysosomal degradation.
source: Thus, rather than preventing the lysosomal degradation of HIF1α, the V-ATPase inhibition stabilised HIF1α by decreasing PHD enzymatic activity.
evidence: Inferred from the in vitro hydroxylation assay results and prolyl-hydroxylation status of HIF1α.

claim: PHDs require Fe(II) and 2-oxoglutarate as cofactors for catalytic activity in addition to molecular oxygen.
source: PHDs are 2-oxoglutarate (2-OG) dependent dioxygenases, which aside from molecular oxygen, require Fe(II) and 2-OG as cofactors for catalytic activity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PHD enzyme biochemistry.

claim: Iron chelators and iron metabolism can alter PHD activity.
source: We focused on iron as: (i) iron chelators and iron metabolism can alter PHD activity (Wang and Semenza, 1993), and (ii) the V-ATPase is implicated in iron homeostasis via clathrin-mediated endocytosis of transferrin (Kozik et al., 2013), the conversion of ferric to ferrous iron within endosomes (Dautry-Varsat et al., 1983; Straud et al., 2010), and the release of iron from ferritin stores (Mancias et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Semenza, 1993.

claim: The V-ATPase is implicated in iron homeostasis via clathrin-mediated endocytosis of transferrin.
source: We focused on iron as: (i) iron chelators and iron metabolism can alter PHD activity (Wang and Semenza, 1993), and (ii) the V-ATPase is implicated in iron homeostasis via clathrin-mediated endocytosis of transferrin (Kozik et al., 2013), the conversion of ferric to ferrous iron within endosomes (Dautry-Varsat et al., 1983; Straud et al., 2010), and the release of iron from ferritin stores (Mancias et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kozik et al., 2013.

claim: The V-ATPase is involved in the conversion of ferric to ferrous iron within endosomes.
source: We focused on iron as: (i) iron chelators and iron metabolism can alter PHD activity (Wang and Semenza, 1993), and (ii) the V-ATPase is implicated in iron homeostasis via clathrin-mediated endocytosis of transferrin (Kozik et al., 2013), the conversion of ferric to ferrous iron within endosomes (Dautry-Varsat et al., 1983; Straud et al., 2010), and the release of iron from ferritin stores (Mancias et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dautry-Varsat et al., 1983 and Straud et al., 2010.

claim: The V-ATPase is involved in the release of iron from ferritin stores.
source: We focused on iron as: (i) iron chelators and iron metabolism can alter PHD activity (Wang and Semenza, 1993), and (ii) the V-ATPase is implicated in iron homeostasis via clathrin-mediated endocytosis of transferrin (Kozik et al., 2013), the conversion of ferric to ferrous iron within endosomes (Dautry-Varsat et al., 1983; Straud et al., 2010), and the release of iron from ferritin stores (Mancias et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mancias et al., 2014.

claim: IRP2 is a sensitive marker of intracellular free iron that accumulates in iron deficient conditions.
source: To examine if V-ATPase inhibition resulted in cytosolic iron depletion, we treated the cells with BafA and measured the levels of IRP2 (also known as IREB2); a sensitive maker of intracellular free iron that is rapidly ubiquitinated and undergoes proteasomal degradation in iron-replete cells, but accumulates in iron deficient conditions (Iwai et al., 1995; Salahudeen et al., 2009; Vashisht et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Iwai et al., 1995; Salahudeen et al., 2009; Vashisht et al., 2009.

claim: BafA treatment stabilizes IRP2 similarly to cells treated with the iron chelator DFO.
source: BafA treatment stabilised IRP2 similarly to cells treated with DFO (Figure 8A), consistent with V-ATPase inhibition leading to depletion of intracellular iron.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: BafA treatment increases NCOA4, the main cargo receptor for ferritinophagy.
source: DFO and particularly BafA treatment also increased NCOA4, the main cargo receptor for the autophagic degradation of ferritin (ferritinophagy) and mobilisation of intracellular iron stores (Mancias et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 8A and citation to Mancias et al., 2014.

claim: While NCOA4 promotes ferritinophagy in DFO treated cells, ferritin levels are unchanged in BafA treated cells, consistent with a complete block in autophagy when the V-ATPase is inhibited.
source: However, while NCOA4 promoted ferritinophagy in DFO treated cells, ferritin levels were unchanged in BafA treated cells, consistent with a complete block in autophagy when the V-ATPase was inhibited (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data showing ferritin levels in Figure 8A.

claim: TMEM199, CCDC115, ATP6V0D1, or ATP6V1A1 deficient cells show increased IRP2 and NCOA4 levels.
source: Similar increases in IRP2 and NCOA4 were observed in FACS GFPHIGH populations of TMEM199, CCDC115, ATP6V0D1 or ATP6V1A1 deficient HIF1α-GFPODD reporter cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Disrupting V-ATPase integrity and assembly results in intracellular iron depletion.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that disrupting V-ATPase integrity and assembly results in intracellular iron depletion.
evidence: Inferred from IRP2 and NCOA4 accumulation data.

claim: Ferrous iron supplementation restores in vitro prolyl hydroxylation in DFO treated lysates.
source: We first validated that ferrous iron restored in vitro prolyl hydroxylation of the HIF1αODD in DFO treated lysates (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro hydroxylation assay data shown in Figures 8C and 8D.

claim: Addition of 1 µM Fe(II) completely restores prolyl hydroxylation of HIF1αODD in BafA treated lysates.
source: We then examined the effect of ferrous iron treatment on PHD activity in extracts from BafA treated HeLa cells (Figure 8E,F). The addition of 1 µM Fe(II) completely restored prolyl hydroxylation of the HIF1αODD (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: Supported by in vitro hydroxylation assay data shown in Figures 8E and 8F.

claim: Iron supplementation with 50 µM Fe(III) citrate completely prevents HIF1α stabilization in BafA treated cells.
source: To explore if iron supplementation was sufficient to restore HIF1α turnover in cells where the V-ATPase had been inhibited, BafA treated HIF1α-GFPODD reporter or wildtype HeLa cells were supplemented with or without 50 µM iron (Fe(III)) citrate for 24 hr, and HIF1α levels measured by flow cytometry and immuoblot (Figure 9A,B). While BafA treatment stabilised the GFP reporter and endogenous HIF1α, this was completely prevented by the addition of iron to the media.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 9A and 9B.

claim: Iron supplementation restores HIF1α turnover in DFO treated cells, although the concentration of iron needed is higher (200 µM Fe(III)) than for BafA treatment.
source: Similar findings were observed in cells treated with DFO and iron citrate (Figure 9C,D), although the concentration of iron needed to restore HIF1α degradation was higher (200 µM Fe(III)).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 9C and 9D.

claim: Iron supplementation restores HIF1α turnover in BafA treated primary human dermal fibroblasts, HEK293ET cells, and RCC10 cells reconstituted with VHL.
source: Iron supplementation also restored HIF1α turnover in BafA treated primary human dermal fibroblasts, HEK293ET cells and RCC10 cells that had been reconstituted with VHL (Figure 9E–G).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 9E-G.

claim: Iron citrate prevents the downstream activation of HIF1 target genes (GLUT1, VEGF, and carbonic anhydrase 9) following BafA treatment without affecting HIF1α mRNA levels.
source: Furthermore, iron citrate also prevented the downstream activation of several HIF1 target genes (GLUT1, VEGF and carbonic anhydrase 9) following BafA treatment without affecting HIF1α mRNA levels (Figure 9J).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 9J.

claim: Iron citrate does not affect HIF1α stabilization following proteasome inhibition or in VHL null RCC10 cells.
source: Consistent with iron supplementation only affecting HIF1α levels following V-ATPase inhibition, iron citrate did not affect HIF1α stabilisation following proteasome inhibition or in VHL null RCC10 cells (Figure 9G,H).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 9G and 9H.

claim: Iron supplementation reverses HIF1α stabilization in mixed KO populations of V-ATPase subunits (TMEM199, CCDC115, or ATP6V1A1).
source: Therefore, iron citrate was supplemented to the media of mixed KO populations of individual V-ATPase subunits (TMEM199, CCDC115 or ATP6V1A1) and HIF1α levels measured by immunoblot (Figure 9K–M). Iron treatment reversed the HIF1α stabilisation in the sgRNA-targeted cells (Figure 9K–M), confirming that iron supplementation was sufficient to restore HIF1α degradation following genetic disruption of the V-ATPase.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 9K-M.

claim: Pre-conditioning the media with iron citrate does not prevent the accumulation of HIF1α following BafA treatment.
source: We examined if treating cells with ferric iron prior to BafA treatment prevented HIF1α accumulation and conversely, also measured if iron supplementation after BafA treatment affected HIF1α levels (Figure 10A). Pre-conditioning the media with iron citrate did not prevent the accumulation of HIF1α following BafA treatment (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Iron supplementation at the time of BafA treatment or after 12 hours decreases HIF1α levels.
source: However, iron supplementation at the time of BafA treatment or after 12 hr did decrease HIF1α levels (Figure 10A), suggesting that iron supplementation restores HIF1α turnover following disruption of the V-ATPase by a transferrin independent mechanism.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Iron supplementation restores HIF1α turnover following V-ATPase disruption by a transferrin independent mechanism.
source: However, iron supplementation at the time of BafA treatment or after 12 hr did decrease HIF1α levels (Figure 10A), suggesting that iron supplementation restores HIF1α turnover following disruption of the V-ATPase by a transferrin independent mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the timing of iron supplementation effects.

claim: Mixed KO populations of NCOA4 cells have no effect on HIF1α levels.
source: To further explore the relative contributions of iron uptake and ferritin turnover to intracellular iron homeostasis, we depleted cells of transferrin receptor, IRP2 or NCOA4 by sgRNA, and used HIF1α stability as a sensitive functional measure of iron levels. Mixed KO populations of NCOA4 cells had no effect on HIF1α levels (Figure 10B,C – Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 10B, 10C, and supplement.

claim: NCOA4 depletion increases IRP2 levels after 12 days, suggesting that IRP2 may increase iron flux through the endosomal pathway.
source: Interestingly, NCOA4 depletion did increase IRP2 levels after 12 days, suggesting that IRP2 may increase iron flux through the endosomal pathway, but cell surface transferrin receptor and total ferritin levels did not change (Figure 10B,C)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 10B and 10C, with interpretation suggesting increased iron flux.

claim: Depletion of either IRP2 or the transferrin receptor stabilizes the HIF1α-GFPODD reporter and endogenous HIF1α, most markedly in transferrin receptor null cells.
source: Depletion of either IPR2 or the transferrin receptor stabilised the HIF1α-GFPODD reporter and endogenous HIF1α, although this was most marked in the transferrin receptor null cells (Figure 10D–F,H – Figure 10—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 10D-F, 10H, and supplements.

claim: IRP2 depletion does not alter cell surface transferrin receptor levels, consistent with IRP2 regulating iron flux rather than just transferrin receptor expression.
source: IRP2 depletion also did not alter cell surface transferrin receptor levels (Figure 10D), consistent with IRP2 regulating iron flux rather than just transferrin receptor expression.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 10D with interpretation about IRP2 function.

claim: Ferritinophagy does not contribute significantly to cytosolic Fe(II) levels when the transferrin pathway is functional.
source: Thus, ferritinophagy does not seem to contribute significantly to cytosolic Fe(II) levels when the transferrin pathway is functional.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of HIF1α stabilization in NCOA4 depleted cells.

claim: Iron treatment decreases HIF1α levels and increases ferritin stores in transferrin receptor deficient cells without altering NCOA4 levels.
source: Mixed transferrin receptor KO populations were treated with iron citrate for 24 hr and HIF1α levels measured. Iron treatment decreased HIF1α levels and increased ferritin stores without altering NCOA4 levels (Figure 10G,H – Figure 10—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and immunoblot data shown in Figures 10G, 10H, and supplement.

claim: When the transferrin pathway is impaired, increasing the availability of extracellular Fe(III) is sufficient to restore PHD activity and HIF1α degradation.
source: Thus, when the transferrin pathway is impaired, either by depletion of the transferrin receptor or disrupting V-ATPase activity, increasing the availability of extracellular Fe(III) is sufficient to restore PHD activity and HIF1α degradation.
evidence: Inferred from iron supplementation rescue experiments in transferrin receptor deficient and V-ATPase inhibited cells.

claim: Homozygous mutations in ATP6V0A3 cause infantile osteopetrosis.
source: Homozygous mutations in a V0 subunit isoform (ATP6V0A3) cause infantile osteopetrosis (failure of bone resorption) (Kornak et al., 2000), while mutations in kidney specific isoforms (ATP6V0A4) cause distal tubular renal acidosis (Karet et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kornak et al., 2000.

claim: Mutations in ATP6V0A4 cause distal tubular renal acidosis.
source: Homozygous mutations in a V0 subunit isoform (ATP6V0A3) cause infantile osteopetrosis (failure of bone resorption) (Kornak et al., 2000), while mutations in kidney specific isoforms (ATP6V0A4) cause distal tubular renal acidosis (Karet et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karet et al., 1999 and Smith et al., 2000.

claim: Several cancer cell types express V-ATPase complexes at the plasma membrane, possibly as a mechanism for regulating cytosolic pH.
source: Furthermore, several cancer cell types express V-ATPase complexes at the plasma membrane (Capecci and Forgac, 2013), possibly as a mechanism for regulating cytosolic pH, which appear to render tumour cells more susceptible to cell death when the V-ATPase is inhibited (Perut et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Capecci and Forgac, 2013 and Perut et al., 2014.

claim: Cancer cells with plasma membrane V-ATPase appear more susceptible to cell death when the V-ATPase is inhibited.
source: Furthermore, several cancer cell types express V-ATPase complexes at the plasma membrane (Capecci and Forgac, 2013), possibly as a mechanism for regulating cytosolic pH, which appear to render tumour cells more susceptible to cell death when the V-ATPase is inhibited (Perut et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perut et al., 2014.

claim: The ability of iron treatment to completely restore HIF1α turnover when the V-ATPase is inhibited argues against a role for CMA in HIF1α regulation.
source: The ability of iron treatment to completely restore HIF1α turnover when the V-ATPase is inhibited, without altering the lysosomal degradation of EGFR or the autophagy cargo receptor NCOA4, also argues against a role for CMA in HIF1α regulation.
evidence: Inferred from the iron rescue experiments showing restoration of HIF1α degradation without affecting lysosomal function.

claim: The requirement for the AAA ATPase P97 in HIF1α degradation suggests that HIF1α may be incorporated into larger complexes that require unfolding prior to proteolysis.
source: The requirement for the AAA ATPase P97 in HIF1α degradation suggests that it may be incorporated into larger complexes that require unfolding prior to proteolysis (Alexandru et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alexandru et al., 2008 and inference about protein complex requirements.

claim: The major consequence of V-ATPase inhibition is stabilization of HIF1α by preventing prolyl hydroxylation.
source: Nevertheless, we find that the major consequence of V-ATPase inhibition is stabilisation of HIF1α by preventing prolyl hydroxylation.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including hydroxylation assays and iron rescue experiments.

claim: The findings are consistent with prior studies showing impaired uptake of transferrin following V-ATPase inhibition.
source: Our findings are consistent with prior studies showing impaired uptake of transferrin following V-ATPase inhibition (Kozik et al., 2013; Straud et al., 2010), and confirm the importance of V-ATPase activity in regulating iron through clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Kozik et al., 2013), endosomal acidification (Eckenroth et al., 2011; Ohgami et al., 2005) and ferritinophagy (Mancias et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on V-ATPase and transferrin uptake.

claim: V-ATPase activity is important for regulating iron through clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: Our findings are consistent with prior studies showing impaired uptake of transferrin following V-ATPase inhibition (Kozik et al., 2013; Straud et al., 2010), and confirm the importance of V-ATPase activity in regulating iron through clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Kozik et al., 2013), endosomal acidification (Eckenroth et al., 2011; Ohgami et al., 2005) and ferritinophagy (Mancias et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kozik et al., 2013 and experimental data in this study.

claim: V-ATPase activity is important for endosomal acidification in the context of iron regulation.
source: Our findings are consistent with prior studies showing impaired uptake of transferrin following V-ATPase inhibition (Kozik et al., 2013; Straud et al., 2010), and confirm the importance of V-ATPase activity in regulating iron through clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Kozik et al., 2013), endosomal acidification (Eckenroth et al., 2011; Ohgami et al., 2005) and ferritinophagy (Mancias et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eckenroth et al., 2011 and Ohgami et al., 2005, and experimental data in this study.

claim: V-ATPase inhibition both alters iron uptake and degradation of ferritin.
source: The V-ATPase is not only implicated in iron uptake and conversion to Fe(II), but also required for the release of iron from ferritin stores via ferritinophagy. Using HIF1α stabilisation as a sensitive marker for intracellular iron, we find that inhibition or disruption of the V-ATPase both alters iron uptake and degradation of ferritin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing effects on both transferrin uptake and ferritin levels.

claim: HIF1α is only stabilized in transferrin receptor deficient cells, implying that increased ferritin turnover is not sufficient to compensate for prolonged loss of transferrin-mediated iron uptake.
source: However, HIF1α was only stabilised in the transferrin receptor deficient cells, implying that increased ferritin turnover is not sufficient to compensate for prolonged loss of transferrin-mediated iron uptake.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of HIF1α levels in NCOA4 vs transferrin receptor depleted cells.

claim: Decreased transferrin uptake and conversion of Fe(III) to Fe(II) are the predominant mechanisms for reduced PHD activity when the V-ATPase is inhibited.
source: These findings are consistent with decreased transferrin uptake and conversion of Fe(III) to Fe(II) being the predominant mechanisms for reduced PHD activity when the V-ATPase is inhibited, and highlight the relative importance of iron uptake versus release from intracellular stores.
evidence: Inferred from the relative effects of transferrin receptor vs NCOA4 depletion on HIF1α levels.

claim: Fe(III) supplementation to the media is sufficient to restore HIF1α turnover when the V-ATPase is inhibited or following depletion of the transferrin receptor.
source: Interestingly, Fe(III) supplementation to the media was sufficient to restore HIF1α turnover when the V-ATPase was inhibited or following depletion of the transferrin receptor.
evidence: Supported by iron supplementation rescue experiments.

claim: Transferrin-independent uptake of iron can occur when there is sufficient extracellular iron availability, presumably by transporters such as Zip14.
source: Thus, transferrin-independent uptake of iron can occur when there is sufficient extracellular iron availability, presumably by transporters such as Zip14, which mediate non-transferrin bound iron uptake (Liuzzi et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from iron rescue experiments and supported by citation to Liuzzi et al., 2006.

claim: HIF activation and V-ATPase activity may serve as a feedback mechanism to control intracellular iron.
source: Moreover, it is plausible that HIF activation and V-ATPase activity serve as a feedback mechanism to control intracellular iron, particularly as HIFs promote genes involved in iron metabolism (Pantopoulos et al., 2012; Peyssonnaux et al., 2008; Simpson and McKie, 2015).
evidence: Speculative inference based on the relationship between HIF and iron metabolism, supported by citations.

claim: HIFs promote genes involved in iron metabolism.
source: Moreover, it is plausible that HIF activation and V-ATPase activity serve as a feedback mechanism to control intracellular iron, particularly as HIFs promote genes involved in iron metabolism (Pantopoulos et al., 2012; Peyssonnaux et al., 2008; Simpson and McKie, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pantopoulos et al., 2012; Peyssonnaux et al., 2008; Simpson and McKie, 2015.

claim: In yeast, Vma12p and Vma22p dimerize and promote the assembly of the membrane embedded V0 complex, which can subsequently associate with the peripheral V1 complex.
source: In yeast, Vma12p and Vma22p dimerise and are thought to promote the assembly of the membrane embedded complex (V0), which can subsequently associate with the peripheral complex (V1) (Graham et al., 1998; Hill and Stevens, 1995; Hirata et al., 1993; Jansen et al., 2016c).
evidence: Supported by citations to yeast studies on V-ATPase assembly.

claim: TMEM199 is predominantly localized to the endoplasmic reticulum, implying it is likely involved in V-ATPase assembly rather than forming part of the mature complex.
source: Similarly to the yeast Vma12 studies, we find that TMEM199 is predominantly localised to the endoplasmic reticulum, implying that it is likely to be involved in V-ATPase assembly, rather than forming part of the mature complex.
evidence: Inferred from localization data and comparison to yeast Vma12p.

claim: Human germline mutations in TMEM199 and CCDC115 cause disorders with a liver storage disease phenotype.
source: Human germline mutations in TMEM199 and CCDC115 cause disorders with a liver storage disease phenotype (Jansen et al., 2016b, 2016c) and it remains to be determined how impaired glycosylation relates to V-ATPase function, or if these defects relate to other roles of TMEM199 and CCDC115.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jansen et al., 2016b and 2016c.

claim: All described TMEM199 and CCDC115 human mutations have impaired glycosylation of transferrin.
source: However, it is of interest that all described TMEM199 and CCDC115 human mutations have impaired glycosylation of transferrin, suggesting a role for the V-ATPase associated factors in iron metabolism (Jansen et al., 2016b, 2016c).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jansen et al., 2016b and 2016c.

claim: ATP6AP1 has been identified as the human orthologue of the yeast Voa1 V-ATPase assembly factor.
source: ATP6AP1 (also known as Ac45) was also identified in our forward genetic screen and has recently been identified as the human orthologue of the yeast Voa1 V-ATPase assembly factor (Jansen et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jansen et al., 2016a.

claim: Human mutations in ATP6AP1 result in immunodeficiency as well as abnormal glycosylation.
source: Human mutations in ATP6AP1 have a distinct phenotype to that of TMEM199 and CCDC115 mutations, resulting in immunodeficiency as well as abnormal glycosylation (Jansen et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jansen et al., 2016a.

claim: Human mutations in VMA21 cause an autophagic myopathy.
source: Furthermore, human mutations in another V-ATPase assembly factor, VMA21, cause an autophagic myopathy (Ramachandran et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramachandran et al., 2013.
